### 1.  Reduce the radicals

Write each integer as a square‑free part times a square:

\[
x=d_{1}u^{2},\qquad y=d_{2}v^{2},
\]

where \(d_{1},d_{2}\) are square–free positive integers and \(u,v\in\mathbb N\).
Then  

\[
\sqrt{x}=u\sqrt{d_{1}},\qquad\sqrt{y}=v\sqrt{d_{2}}
\]

and the equation becomes  

\[
\frac{3}{u\sqrt{d_{1}}}+\frac{2}{v\sqrt{d_{2}}}= \frac1{\sqrt2 } .
\tag{1}
\]

Multiply (1) by \(\sqrt2\):

\[
\frac{3\sqrt2}{u\sqrt{d_{1}}}+\frac{2\sqrt2}{v\sqrt{d_{2}}}=1 .
\tag{2}
\]

The numbers \(\sqrt{2/d_{1}}\) and \(\sqrt{2/d_{2}}\) are either rational or irrational.
If either of the radicands is not a perfect square, the two terms on the left of (2) are
linearly independent over \(\mathbb Q\); they cannot sum to the rational number \(1\).
Hence both radicands must be rational, i.e.

\[
\frac{2}{d_{1}}\in\mathbb Q\text{ a square},\qquad 
\frac{2}{d_{2}}\in\mathbb Q\text{ a square}.
\]

Because \(d_{1},d_{2}\) are square‑free, the only possibility is  

\[
d_{1}=d_{2}=2 .
\]

Thus  

\[
x=2u^{2},\qquad y=2v^{2}\qquad (u,v\in\mathbb N).
\]

--------------------------------------------------------------------
### 2.  Obtain a Diophantine equation for \(u\) and \(v\)

Substituting \(\sqrt{x}=u\sqrt2,\;\sqrt{y}=v\sqrt2\) into the original equation gives

\[
\frac{3}{u\sqrt2}+\frac{2}{v\sqrt2}= \frac1{\sqrt2}\;\Longrightarrow\;
\frac{3}{u}+\frac{2}{v}=1 .
\]

Multiplying by \(uv\),

\[
3v+2u=uv .
\]

Rewrite it as

\[
uv-2u-3v=0\quad\Longrightarrow\quad (u-3)(v-2)=6 .
\tag{3}
\]

--------------------------------------------------------------------
### 3.  Solve \((u-3)(v-2)=6\) in positive integers

All factorisations of \(6\) into two positive integers are

\[
1\cdot6,\;2\cdot3,\;3\cdot2,\;6\cdot1 .
\]

Hence

\[
\begin{array}{c|c|c}
u-3 & v-2 & (u,v)\\ \hline
1   & 6   & (4,8)\\
2   & 3   & (5,5)\\
3   & 2   & (6,4)\\
6   & 1   & (9,3)
\end{array}
\]

--------------------------------------------------------------------
### 4.  Return to \((x,y)\)

Recall \(x=2u^{2},\;y=2v^{2}\).  Substituting the four pairs \((u,v)\) yields

\[
\begin{aligned}
(u,v)=(4,8) &\;\Rightarrow\; (x,y)=(2\cdot4^{2},\,2\cdot8^{2})=(32,128),\\
(u,v)=(5,5) &\;\Rightarrow\; (x,y)=(50,50),\\
(u,v)=(6,4) &\;\Rightarrow\; (x,y)=(72,32),\\
(u,v)=(9,3) &\;\Rightarrow\; (x,y)=(162,18).
\end{aligned}
\]

Each pair indeed satisfies \(\displaystyle \frac{3}{\sqrt{x}}+\frac{2}{\sqrt{y}}=\frac{1}{\sqrt2}\).

--------------------------------------------------------------------
\[
\boxed{(x,y)\in\{(32,128),\ (50,50),\ (72,32),\ (162,18)\}}
\]

These four ordered pairs are the only integer solutions of the given equation.<|eot_id|> <|end_of_text|>
